Explanation:

• For amalgam restoration the gingival margin is beveled at 15 – 20° whereas for cast restorations it is beveled at 30 –40°.

The facial and lingual walls of the proximal box are extended such that they clear the adjacent tooth by 0.2 – 0.3mm. The facial and lingual walls are placed in their respective embrasures.

Option B: Round and elongated in the dentin
Option C: Round and short in the dentin
Option D: Sharp and elongated in the dentin
Explanation:
'B' [Sturdevant 5th SA ed 382/ 5th ed 748]
Locks for amalgam and the grooves for cast metal restorations provide additional retention for proximal portions of tooth preparations. They also increase the resistance form. These are placed in the axiofacial and axiolingual line angles 0.2mm inside the DEJ. They are started at the axiofaciogingival (or axio linguo gingival) point angle and terminated at the axio facio pulpal (or axio linguo pulpal) point angle.

High copper amalgam alloys (that include occlusal dovetail) does not require locks in preparation as they exhibit less creep.

Preventive measures such as fluorides, oral hygiene, proper diet and use of enameloplasty, pit and fissure sealants makes 'constriction for conservation' possible excluding the need for 'extension for prevention'.

'B' [Sturdevant 5th SA ed 47/ 5th ed 291]
Infected dentin has bacteria and collagen that is irreversibly denatured. It is not remineralizable and must be removed. Affected dentin has no bacteria, the collagen is reversibly denatured and remineralizable. It is dark brown in colour, hard in texture and should not be excavated.

1% acid red solution in 0.2% propylene glycol discloses infected dentin.

Question: Which is correct regarding Etching of enamel?
Option A: more time required to etch primary teeth because enamel is more dense than permanent teeth
Option B: Less time required to etch primary teeth because enamel rods are irregularly arranged than permanent teeth
Option C: more time required to etch primary teeth because enamel rods are irregularly arranged than permanent teeth
Option D: more time required to etch primary teeth because of more prismless enamel and rods are irregularly arranged than permanent teeth
Explanation:
'D' [Philips 11th ed 383]
Primary enamel exhibits the following morphological differences compared to permanent teeth enamel:
• More prismless or interprismatic substance
• It is less-mineralized than permanent enamel
• the diffusion coefficient is greater in primary than in permanent
• less mineral density

Primary teeth require more etching time due to the presence of more prismless or interprismatic substance at the surface. It takes longer for the acid to penetrate the prismless layer to create the etch pattern on the underlying prismatic enamel.
